previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: A 58-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes, chronic systolic heart failure, and bilateral below-knee amputations was admitted for acute renal failure and hyperkalemia discovered during a clinic visit. She was treated for a urinary tract infection caused by Citrobacter freundii, initially with meropenem and later switched to ciprofloxacin based on culture results. Her hyperkalemia resolved with medical management, and her renal function improved with hydration and antibiotics. Due to recurrent UTIs and incomplete bladder emptying, a Foley catheter was placed, and she was referred to urology for clean intermittent catheterization training. She underwent a right BKA revision for a nonhealing ulcer, which healed well. Medication adjustments included increasing metoprolol, starting lisinopril, stopping fluconazole, and reducing vancomycin dose. She was discharged home with nursing services, stable and afebrile, with follow-up arranged across multiple specialties.

Brief Hospital Course:
___ year old female multiple medical problems including type 1 
diabetes, peripheral vascular disease s/p BKA with multiple 
revisions (most recently ___ and wound infections, ESBL 
klebsiella urosepsis, C.diffile colitis presents with fever and 
hypotension.
.
#SEPSIS: She was admitted to the medical ICU given her SIRS 
criteria (fever, leukocytosis) and hypotension concerning for 
septic shock. There was suspicion of urinary source of infection 
given her risk factors and history of multi-drug resistant 
organisms. She was continued on broad spectrum antibiotics. Her 
foley catheter was changed. The hypotension was fluid responsive 
and she did not require vasopressors. Her antibiotics were 
narrowed to Meropenem and PO vancomycin to prevent C. Diff 
colitis given her history. Her urine ultiamtely grew 
pan-resistant Klebsiella Pneumonia.  Even though her urine was 
not sensitive to meropenem, she improved and had no further 
fevers. ID was consulted for this complicated infection. She 
completed an entire 7 day course of antibiotics for her UTI.

#Urinary Incontinence: Neurogenic Bladder Dysfunction from 
diabetes has put patient at higher risk for developed recurrent 
UTIs. Urology was called and will meet with her outpatient to 
teach her CIC and learn to self-catheterize herself to decrease 
her UTIs. Urology will also present the idea of an appendicela 
conduit if patient continues to get repeated UTIs. Pt went home 
with diapers until her appointment with urology in 1 day.
.
#HISTORY OF C. DIFF COLITIS: She was noted to have large volumes 
of stool, although this was after receiving kayexcelate. C. 
difficile was sent and returned negative. She was continued 
emperically on PO vancomycin while she was on antibiotics. 
.
#ACUTE RENAL FAILURE: Baseline creatinine of 1.1-1.2 with 
elevated creatinine to 1.5. Likely pre-renal in setting of 
fever, poor po. Her Cr dropped with fluid hydration and it was 
0.9 on day of discharge.
.
#HYPERKALEMIA: Pt's K was elevated on admission, most likely ___ 
ARF and lisinopril. Lisinopril was held. Cr improved with IVF.
.  
#DIABETES: Patient had several episodes of hyperglycemia up to 
the 400s and hypoglycemia down to the ___. She was put on an 
insulin sliding scale throughout her hospitalization with 
adjusted parameters based on her glucose level. Pt has history 
of brittle diabetes per OMR notes, likely explaining her range 
of glucose levels. Pt told to continue her home insulin regimen 
and follow with ___.
.
#HYPERTENSION: Her home metoprolol and lisinopril were initially 
held in seting of SIRS on admission. Metoprolol and lisinopril 
were added back after pts BP normalized.
.
#NEUROPATHY: Continued her home medications for neuropathy.

Discharge Instructions:
It was a pleasure to care for you during your hospilization here 
at ___.

You were admitted for a serious infection in your urinary tract 
that caused your body to drop it's pressure. You were initially 
sent to the Intensive Care Unit until you stabalized. You were 
started on broad spectrum antibiotics to eliminate your urinary 
tract infection. You were treated with 7 days of Meropenem 
antibiotic through your veins.
The vascular surgeons examined the wounds on your leg and felt 
that they were healing well and that they were not the source of 
your infection.
You got better during your hospitalization and stopped having 
fevers.

The Urology doctors saw ___ and ___ you try a new way to 
eliminate urine called: self catheterization. They look forward 
to teaching you this technique at an appointment on ___. By 
self-catheterizing yourself, you will eliminate your risk of 
having recurrent urinary tract infections. For now, please wear 
daily diapers to collect your urine until your urology 
appointment.

You will see the infectious disease doctors in ___ days. 
Beforehand, you must give a urine and  blood culture specimen 
___ days after your discharge from the hospital. Idealy you 
would do this tomorrow, ___ which is the same day 
as your Urology appointment. Please bring the attached form with 
the presciption to get a urine culture and urine analysis along 
with a blood culture. You can get these labs drawn in the 
___ building on the day of your Urology appointment.

The following changes were made to your medications:
-Your blood pressure medications (Metoprolol and Lisinopril) 
were initially held when you were acutely sick. They were 
re-introduced during your hosptialization. You must continue to 
take these medications every day.
-Your gabapentin was held during your hospitalization. You can 
continue this medicine when you leave the hospital.
-Your trazadone was not given to you during your 
hospitalization. We gave you Zolpidem to help you sleep. You can 
continue your normal sleep regimen when you go home.

Please continue all of your normal home medications, including 
your normal insulin regimen. 

At this point, you will not go home on any further antibiotics. 
You will have an appointment with your infectious disease doctor 
in the next few weeks to monitor you carefully for signs of 
infection.

It is very important to continue your medications every day as 
well as your daily wound dressing changes. Your dressing changes 
only require dry gauze to any wound that is oozing. All other 
wounds can be open to the air.

Please make sure you follow up with your primary care doctor, 
your infectious disease doctor, your new urologist and your 
vascular doctor.

radiology_notes.text:
INDICATION:  Fever.

COMPARISON:  ___.

PA AND LATERAL VIEWS OF THE CHEST:  Mild cardiomegaly is stable.  Mediastinal
and hilar contours are normal.  Linear opacity over the medial left
hemidiaphragm is stable, reflecting atelectasis or scar.  There is no pleural
effusion or pneumothorax.   Faint linear medial right upper lobe opacities are
improved from the comparison study, consistent with resolving consolidation or
resolved consolidation with residual atelectasis/scar.  An IVC filter is
unchanged.

INDICATION:  Central line placement, now with sepsis.

COMPARISON:  ___.

SINGLE BEDSIDE FRONTAL RADIOGRAPH OF THE CHEST:  A left subclavian central
venous line is new, with the tip terminating in the upper portion of the right
atrium.  There is no pneumothorax or pleural effusion.  Mild cardiomegaly is
stable.  Mediastinal and hilar contours are also stable.  As before note is
made of an IVC filter.

HISTORY:  Urinary tract infection.

Two views.  Comparison with the previous study done ___.  Streaky density
in the left lower lobe and right upper lobe persist.  The lungs appear
otherwise clear.  The heart appears enlarged, although cardiac size may be
exaggerated by AP technique.  Mediastinal structures are otherwise
unremarkable.  The bony thorax is grossly intact.  A left subclavian catheter
remains in place.

IMPRESSION:  Subsegmental atelectasis and/or scarring.  Cardiomegaly.  No
significant change.

CT ABDOMEN AND PELVIS WITHOUT CONTRAST

INDICATION:  ___ woman with diabetes, peripheral vascular disease,
status post bilateral below knee amputations, recurrent UTIs.  Assess for
kidney stones.

COMPARISON:  CTU with and without contrast, ___.

TECHNIQUE:  Axial MDCT images were acquired from the lung bases to the
symphysis pubis in the absence of intravenous contrast.  Coronal and sagittal
reformats were produced and reviewed.

FINDINGS:

CT ABDOMEN WITHOUT CONTRAST:

Linear atelectasis or scarring seen at both lung bases, this is unchanged
compared with previous study.  Non-contrast examination of the liver makes it
difficult to assess the hypoenhancing lesion previously identified in segment
VIII, although it is still seen to be present.  No new hepatic lesions
identified.  Multiple calculi are seen within the gallbladder, no evidence of
cholecystitis.  The spleen is unremarkable in appearance.  There are numerous
small calcifications evident at both renal hila.  The majority of these appear
to be vascular in distribution.  There is a 1.2 cm hypoattenuating lesion seen
in the interpolar region of the right kidney.  This was previously seen to be
consistent with a cyst on post-contrast imagimg.  Adjacent to this, there is a
0.2 cm calcification, which may represent a small renal calculus.  This is not
causing any obstruction.  No hydronephrosis seen.  Quite extensive
calcification of the abdominal aorta, iliac vessels and femoral vessels.  IVC
filter in situ in adequate position.  No free fluid seen.  No intra-abdominal
lymphadenopathy seen.  

CT PELVIS WITHOUT CONTRAST:

The bladder is distended; however, the bladder wall appears slightly thickened
when compared to the previous study.  This suggests the possibility of
cystitis, although it is not diagnostic.  There is a small pocket of air seen
anteriorly within the bladder.  If the patient has had recent instrumentation
including catheterization, this would account for the air within the bladder. 
However, in the absence of recent instrumentation, this raises the possibility
of cystitis with gas forming organism.

OSSEOUS STRUCTURES:  No concerning lytic or sclerotic bony lesion seen.

IMPRESSION:

1.  Multiple tiny calcifications at the renal hila are most likely vascular. 
Possible small calculus in the right kidney, which is not causing any
obstruction.

2.  Thick-walled bladder with intraluminal air, which may be due to recent
instrumentation but could also be due to chronic cystitis.
